In modern [[computer science]] and [[statistics]], the '''complexity index''' of a function denotes the level of informational content, which in turn affects the difficulty of learning the [[supervised learning|function from examples]]. This is different from [[Analysis of algorithms|computational complexity]], which is the difficulty to compute a function. '''Complexity indices''' characterize the entire class of functions to which the one we are interested in belongs. Focusing on [[Boolean function]]s, the ''detail'' of a class <math>\mathsf C</math> of Boolean functions ''c'' essentially denotes how deeply the class is articulated.

==Technical definition==
To identify this index we must first define a ''sentry function'' of <math>\mathsf C</math>.
Let us focus for a moment on a single function ''c'', call it a ''concept'' defined on a set <math>\mathcal X</math> of elements that we may figure as points in a [[Euclidean space]]. In this framework, the above function associates to ''c'' a set of points that, since are defined to be external to the concept, prevent it from expanding into another function of <math>\mathsf C</math>. We may dually define these points  in terms of sentinelling a given concept ''c'' from being fully enclosed (invaded) by another concept within the class. Therefore, we call these points either ''sentinels'' or ''sentry points''; they are assigned by the sentry function <math>\boldsymbol S</math> to each concept of <math>\mathsf C</math> in such a way that:
# the sentry points are external to the concept ''c'' to be sentineled and internal to at least one other including it,
# each concept <math>c'</math> including ''c'' has at least one of the sentry points of ''c'' either in the gap between ''c'' and <math>c'</math>, or outside <math>c'</math> and distinct from the sentry points of <math>c'</math>, and
# they constitute a minimal set with these properties.

The technical definition coming from {{harv|Apolloni|2006}} is rooted in the inclusion of an augmented concept <math>c^+</math> made up of ''c'' plus its sentry points by another <math>\left(c'\right)^+</math> in the same class.

== Definition of sentry function ==
For a concept class <math>\mathsf C</math> on a space <math>\mathfrak X</math>, a ''sentry function'' is a [[total function]] <math>\boldsymbol S: \mathsf C\cup\{\emptyset,\mathfrak X\}\mapsto 2^{\mathfrak X}</math> satisfying the following conditions:
# Sentinels are outside the sentineled concept <big>(</big><math>c\cap{\boldsymbol S}(c)=\emptyset</math> for all <math>c\in \mathsf C</math><big>)</big>.
# Sentinels are inside the invading concept <big>(</big>Having introduced the sets <math>c^+=c\cup\boldsymbol S(c)</math>, an invading concept <math>c'\in \mathsf C</math> is such that <math>c'\not\subseteq c</math> and <math>c^+\subseteq \left(c'\right)^+</math>. Denoting <math>\mathrm{up}(c)</math> the set of concepts invading ''c'', we must have that if <math>c_2\in\mathrm{up}(c_1)</math>, then <math>c_2\cap{\boldsymbol S}(c_1)\neq\emptyset</math><big>)</big>.
# <math>{\boldsymbol S}(c)</math> is a minimal set with the above properties <big>(</big>No <math>{\boldsymbol S}'\neq{\boldsymbol S}</math> exists satisfying (1) and (2) and having the property that <math>\boldsymbol S'(c)\subseteq \boldsymbol S(c)</math> for every <math>c\in \mathsf C</math><big>)</big>.
# Sentinels are honest guardians. It may be that <math>c\subseteq \left(c'\right)^+</math> but <math>{\boldsymbol S} (c)\cap c'=\emptyset</math> so that <math>c'\not\in\mathrm{up}(c)</math>. This however must be a consequence of the fact that all points of <math>{\boldsymbol S}(c)</math> are involved in really sentineling ''c'' against other concepts in <math>\mathrm{up}(c)</math> and not just in avoiding inclusion of <math>c^+</math> by <math>(c')^+</math>. Thus if we remove <math>c', {\boldsymbol S}(c)</math> remains unchanged <big>(</big>Whenever <math>c_1</math> and <math>c_2</math> are such that <math>c_1\subset c_2\cup{\boldsymbol S}(c_2)</math> and <math>c_2\cap{\boldsymbol S}(c_1)=\emptyset</math>, then the restriction of <math>{\boldsymbol S}</math> to <math>\{c_1\}\cup\mathrm{up}(c_1)-\{c_2\}</math> is a sentry function on this set<big>)</big>.

<math>{\boldsymbol S}(c)</math> is the ''frontier'' of ''c'' upon <math>\boldsymbol S</math>.

[[File:SentinelEx.png|thumb|right|260px|A schematic outlook of outer sentineling functionality]]

With reference to the picture on the right, <math>\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}</math> is a candidate frontier of <math>c_0</math> against <math>c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4</math>. All points are in the gap between a <math>c_i</math> and <math>c_0</math>. They  avoid inclusion of <math>c_0\cup\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}</math> in <math>c_3</math>, provided that these points are not used by the latter for sentineling itself against other concepts. ''Vice versa'' we expect that <math>c_1</math> uses <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_3</math> as its own sentinels, <math>c_2</math> uses  <math>x_2</math> and <math>x_3</math> and <math>c_4</math> uses  <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math> analogously. Point <math>x_4</math> is not allowed as a <math>c_0</math> sentry point since, like any diplomatic seat, it should be located outside all other concepts just to ensure that it is not occupied in case of invasion by <math>c_0</math>.

=== Definition of detail ===
{{Anchor|Detail}}The frontier size of the most expensive concept to be sentineled with the least efficient sentineling function, i.e. the quantity

:<math>\mathrm D_{\mathsf C}=\sup_{{\boldsymbol S},c}\#{\boldsymbol S}(c)</math>,

is called ''detail'' of <math>\mathsf C</math>.  <math>\boldsymbol S</math> spans also over sentry functions on subsets of <math>\mathfrak X</math> sentineling in this case the intersections of the concepts with these subsets. Actually, proper subsets of <math>\mathfrak X</math> may host sentineling tasks that prove harder than those emerging with <math>\mathfrak X</math> itself.

The detail <math>\mathrm D_{\mathsf C}</math> is a complexity measure of concept classes dual to the [[VC dimension]] <math>\mathrm D_{\mathsf VC}</math>. The former uses points to separate sets of concepts, the latter concepts for partitioning sets of points. In particular the following inequality holds {{harv|Apolloni|1997}}

:<math>\mathrm D_{\mathsf C}\leq \mathrm D_{\mathsf VC}+1</math>

See also  [[Rademacher complexity]] for a recently introduced class complexity index.

=== Example: continuous spaces ===
Class ''C'' of circles in <math>\mathbb R^2</math> has detail <math>\mathrm D_{\mathsf C}=2</math>, as shown in the picture on left below. Similarly, for the class of segments on <math>\mathbb R</math>, as shown in the picture on right.

|-

| [[File:SentinelSegment.png|thumb|left|260px|The class of segments in <math>\mathbb R</math> and two points needed to sentinel its concepts]]
|}

A worst case {{math|S}}, as illustrated, is: <math>\mathbf S(c_1)=\{x_1,x_2\}, \mathbf S(c_2)=\{x_1\}, \mathbf S(c_3)=\{x_2\}, \mathbf S(c_4)=\emptyset</math>.
